newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - German data put ball in U.S. court.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - German data put ball in U.S. court.

text.p: Surprisingly strong economic data from Germany in January have put any speculation of an interest rate cut on ice, giving U.S. Treasuries the chance to outperform Bunds in the short term, analysts said on Thursday.

But investors need to move fast to make any mileage from the data. Treasuries will have troubles of their own in the next few weeks as Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan delivers his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony and the Fed meets to discuss policy.
"It looks as though the upside potential for Bunds is limited near-term," said IBJ International's Keith Edmonds.

The Bundesbank reported earlier that M3 money supply grew at an annualised rate of 11.7 percent versus its average in the fourth quarter of 1996 and 8.6 percent versus its average in the fourth quarter of 1995.
The Bundesbank said the data were boosted by a strong statistical "overhang" at the end of 1996, including weak money capital formation and strong bank lending to the public sector.

But the German IFO economics institute also reported an upturn in business outlook. Its west German business conditions index rose to 93.6 in January from 89.6 in Decmeber and its business climate index to 93.3 in Janury from 90.9 in December.
Analysts said statistical glitches could explain some of the growth in money supply but overall the data were strong and would keep the Bundesbank from shifting interest rates.
The German repo rate is at 3.0 percent and its discount rate at 2.5 percent. The U.S. federal funds rate is at 5.25 percent and its discount rate at 5.0 percent.

"What we're seeing is data emerging from Germany that suggests the Bundesbank will keep interest rates on hold," said Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ. He said the German data would help push the 10-year T-note/Bund spread to around 80 to 75 basis points in the short term from around 89 now.
But beyond there, the gains for Treasuries would be limited, analysts said.

Fed chairman Alan Greenspan presents his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to the Senate Banking Committee on February 26 and analysts expect he could drop strong hints U.S. inflation is starting to cook. Then there is the Federal Open Market Committee meeting on March 25.

Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London, said both events would keep the U.S. market jittery and Greenspan's testimony would likely foreshadow any U.S. interest rate rise at the end of March.
He said chances for that were 50-50.
Against such a backdrop, Bevan said it was too early to switch into Treasuries from Bunds. He would instead sell Bunds when the market appeared to be bottoming out.
"What we are looking to do is to go outright short in Bunds," said Bevan.
Edmonds at IBJ said the T-note/Bund gap would swing back in Bunds' favour longer term to around 100 basis points.
Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Captial Markets in London, added that bottom might now be approaching with the data showing obvious sparks of life.
"In big picture terms, we're still big fans of Bunds' outperformance but I'm beginning to wonder whether we are near a top at 95 (basis points on the spread)," he said.
But Roberts said any German recovery, weighted down by soaring unemployment and the committment to European monetary union, would be gradual and spread movements moreso.
